blocks.content: Imagine an e-commerce application that needs to process a customer's order. After receiving the order, the application calls a payment service to charge the customer's card.

Normally, the payment service responds within a few hundred milliseconds. However, one day the payment service becomes slow due to a database issue and stops responding. If the e-commerce application keeps waiting indefinitely, the request thread remains blocked, consuming memory, CPU resources, and a connection from the thread pool. As more customer requests arrive, more threads become stuck waiting for the same slow dependency.

Eventually, the application runs out of available resources and becomes unresponsive, even though the original problem existed only in the payment service. To prevent this situation, distributed systems impose a maximum waiting period on every operation.
If the response does not arrive within that period, the operation is aborted and treated as a failure, allowing the system to recover gracefully and continue serving other requests.
1. What is a Timeout?
A timeout is a mechanism that limits how long a system waits for an operation to complete. If the operation exceeds the configured time limit, it is automatically terminated and an error is returned.
Timeouts are essential when communicating with databases, APIs, microservices, and other external systems where delays or failures can occur.
By failing fast instead of waiting indefinitely, they prevent resource exhaustion, improve responsiveness, and stop slow dependencies from causing cascading failures across the system.
This lesson covers the four types of timeouts, deadline propagation, adaptive timeouts, and common mistakes when configuring them.
2. The Four Timeout Types

Every network operation has several distinct phases where things can stall. A single "timeout" value conflates them all which is why most HTTP clients and database drivers expose four separate knobs, each governing a different phase of the call.

["Connect Timeout: Limits how long the client waits to establish a connection with the server (TCP handshake). If the connection cannot be established within this time, the request fails.
","Write Timeout: Limits how long the client can spend sending the request data to the server. This is important for large request bodies or slow networks.
","Read Timeout: Limits how long the client waits to receive data from the server after the request has been sent. If no data arrives within the timeout period, the request fails.
","Response Timeout: Limits the total time allowed to receive the complete response from the server, from the first byte to the last byte.
","Overall Deadline: A global timeout that caps the entire end-to-end operation. Even if individual timeouts have not been exceeded, the request is terminated once the overall deadline is reached.
"]
items: Connect Timeout: Limits how long the client waits to establish a connection with the server (TCP handshake). If the connection cannot be established within this time, the request fails.
Write Timeout: Limits how long the client can spend sending the request data to the server. This is important for large request bodies or slow networks.
Read Timeout: Limits how long the client waits to receive data from the server after the request has been sent. If no data arrives within the timeout period, the request fails.
Response Timeout: Limits the total time allowed to receive the complete response from the server, from the first byte to the last byte.
Overall Deadline: A global timeout that caps the entire end-to-end operation. Even if individual timeouts have not been exceeded, the request is terminated once the overall deadline is reached.

blocks.content: 3. Connect timeout

The connect timeout governs the TCP handshake phase how long to wait for the remote server to accept the connection before giving up. If the server is down, unreachable, or firewalled, this is where the call stalls.

It should be short: 1–5 seconds for services in the same data centre, up to 10 seconds for cross-region calls. A connection that has not been established in 5 seconds almost certainly will not succeed.

blocks.content: 4. Read timeout

The read timeout governs inactivity between bytes arriving after the connection is established. It fires if the server accepts the connection and starts responding, but then goes silent for longer than the threshold most commonly because the server is overloaded mid-response.
Crucially, the read timeout resets on every byte received. A 10-second read timeout on a slow streaming endpoint will not fire if the server keeps sending data, even slowly.

blocks.content: 5. Overall deadline
The overall deadline caps the total elapsed time for an operation, regardless of how many individual timeouts fired or how many retries occurred.
This is the single most important timeout in any service because it bounds the worst-case latency a caller will ever experience.
Without it, three retries each with a 10-second read timeout can hold a thread for 30 seconds.
Future-based Overall Deadline

blocks.content: 6. Deadline propagation
When Service A calls Service B which calls Service C, each service has its own timeout. But what matters to the original caller is the end-to-end budget.

Deadline propagation means passing the remaining time budget from caller to callee so that downstream services automatically shorten their own timeouts to fit what is left instead of each service blindly using its own default and potentially adding up to far longer than the original budget allows.

blocks.content: 7. Adaptive timeouts

Static timeout values are a guess made at development time. Adaptive timeouts set the timeout based on observed recent latency typically the 99th percentile of recent call times, plus a safety margin.
This means timeouts automatically tighten when the upstream is fast and loosen when it is legitimately slow, without requiring a configuration change.
Adaptive Timeout Flow

["Collect latency metrics from recent requests using a histogram.","Calculate the 99th percentile (P99) latency from the histogram.","Multiply the P99 latency by a safety factor (multiplier) to determine the timeout.","Ensure the calculated timeout stays within the configured minimum and maximum limits.","Return the computed adaptive timeout value.","Before executing an operation, calculate the current adaptive timeout.","Execute the task asynchronously using CompletableFuture.","Apply the computed timeout using orTimeout().","If the task completes within the timeout, return the result.","If the task exceeds the timeout, automatically fail the operation with a timeout exception.","Continuously adjust future timeout values based on the latest latency measurements."]
items: Collect latency metrics from recent requests using a histogram.
Calculate the 99th percentile (P99) latency from the histogram.
Multiply the P99 latency by a safety factor (multiplier) to determine the timeout.
Ensure the calculated timeout stays within the configured minimum and maximum limits.
Return the computed adaptive timeout value.
Before executing an operation, calculate the current adaptive timeout.
Execute the task asynchronously using CompletableFuture.
Apply the computed timeout using orTimeout().
If the task completes within the timeout, return the result.
If the task exceeds the timeout, automatically fail the operation with a timeout exception.
Continuously adjust future timeout values based on the latest latency measurements.

blocks.content: 8. Timeout values by context

["Same data centre (LAN) Connect: 200–500ms. Read: 1–5s. Overall: 2–10s. Sub-millisecond RTT any longer means something is wrong.
","Cross-region / WAN Connect: 2–5s. Read: 5–15s. Overall: 10–30s. Account for 50–200ms baseline RTT plus processing.
","External payment / third-party API Connect: 5s. Read: 15–30s. Overall: 30s. External SLAs often allow up to 30s; cap to protect your own SLA.
","Database query Statement timeout: 1–10s for OLTP. Longer only for batch/analytics. Always set socket timeout separately from statement timeout.
","User-facing request Overall deadline: 200–500ms for interactive UI. 2–5s absolute maximum before the user perceives the page as broken.
","Background / async jobs Per-step timeout: 30s–5min. Overall job timeout: depends on SLA. Set both a step can stall even if the job has time left.
"]

User-facing request Overall deadline: 200–500ms for interactive UI. 2–5s absolute maximum before the user perceives the page as broken.

blocks.content: 9. Design rules

["Always set all four timeouts explicitly. Every HTTP client and DB driver ships with a default that is either infinite or far too long. Treat every unconfigured timeout as a future outage waiting to happen.
","Set an overall deadline, not just per-call timeouts. Per-call timeouts let retries stack up. The overall deadline is the single ceiling that bounds worst-case latency regardless of retries.
","Propagate deadlines downstream. Pass the remaining budget to every downstream call. A service that has already used 4 of its 5 seconds should give its database client a 1-second budget, not its default 30 seconds.
","Log the timeout value alongside the error. A timeout exception with no context tells you nothing. Log which upstream timed out, the configured timeout, and the actual elapsed time essential for tuning.
","Never catch TimeoutException and silently return null or a default. A timeout that is swallowed looks like a success to the caller. The caller proceeds as if the operation succeeded, with incorrect data or missing state.
","Never set timeouts longer than the caller's SLA. If your API must respond in 500ms, no downstream call timeout should exceed 400ms you need some budget for your own processing and network overhead.
","Check whether the operation is idempotent before retrying a timeout. A timeout means the server may or may not have acted. Retrying without an idempotency key can cause duplicate side effects.
"]
items: Always set all four timeouts explicitly. Every HTTP client and DB driver ships with a default that is either infinite or far too long. Treat every unconfigured timeout as a future outage waiting to happen.
Set an overall deadline, not just per-call timeouts. Per-call timeouts let retries stack up. The overall deadline is the single ceiling that bounds worst-case latency regardless of retries.

Propagate deadlines downstream. Pass the remaining budget to every downstream call. A service that has already used 4 of its 5 seconds should give its database client a 1-second budget, not its default 30 seconds.

Log the timeout value alongside the error. A timeout exception with no context tells you nothing. Log which upstream timed out, the configured timeout, and the actual elapsed time essential for tuning.

Never catch TimeoutException and silently return null or a default. A timeout that is swallowed looks like a success to the caller. The caller proceeds as if the operation succeeded, with incorrect data or missing state.
Never set timeouts longer than the caller's SLA. If your API must respond in 500ms, no downstream call timeout should exceed 400ms you need some budget for your own processing and network overhead.
Check whether the operation is idempotent before retrying a timeout. A timeout means the server may or may not have acted. Retrying without an idempotency key can cause duplicate side effects.

blocks.content: 10. Common mistakes

Mistake 1: no timeout at all The most dangerous configuration. Any library method call that involves a network socket has a default timeout of "wait forever" unless you explicitly set one. A single hung connection holds a thread, exhausts the connection pool, and takes down the service. Default to explicit timeouts on every external call, no exceptions.

Mistake 2: one giant timeout for everything Setting a single 30-second timeout on an HTTP client and using it for both a fast health-check endpoint and a slow bulk export makes both timeouts wrong. Fast calls should time out fast; slow calls need their own budget. Separate clients or per-request timeout configuration.

Mistake 3: timeout without cancellation Catching the timeout, throwing aTimeoutExceptionto the caller, but leaving the underlying work still running wastes threads, database connections, and CPU. Always cancel the underlying task or interrupt the blocking call when the timeout fires.

Mistake 4: ignoring the deadline when entering a retry loop A retry loop with three attempts and a 10-second per-attempt timeout can run for 30 seconds. If the caller's deadline was 5 seconds, you have already exceeded it on the second attempt. Check the remaining deadline before every retry attempt, not just at the start.

Mistake 5: socket timeout vs statement timeout confusion (databases) Most JDBC drivers have two separate concepts: the socket timeout (how long to wait for bytes from the DB server over TCP) and the query statement timeout (how long the DB server allows the query to execute). Both must be set. Setting only the statement timeout still leaves you exposed to infinite waits on TCP-level stalls.
11. Quick reference

["Connect timeout Caps the TCP handshake. Short: 1–5s. A failed connect almost never succeeds with more time.
","Read timeout Inactivity between bytes received. Resets on each byte. Protects against slow or stalled responses mid-stream.
","Overall deadline Single ceiling on the entire operation including retries. The most important timeout in any service.
","Deadline propagation Pass remaining budget to every downstream call. Prevents downstream defaults from blowing the caller's SLA.
","Adaptive timeout Set at p99 × multiplier of recent latency. Automatically tracks normal variance without manual tuning.
","On timeout fire Cancel the work, log with context, throw a named exception, and check idempotency before any retry.
"]

Read timeout Inactivity between bytes received. Resets on each byte. Protects against slow or stalled responses mid-stream.
Overall deadline Single ceiling on the entire operation including retries. The most important timeout in any service.
Deadline propagation Pass remaining budget to every downstream call. Prevents downstream defaults from blowing the caller's SLA.
Adaptive timeout Set at p99 × multiplier of recent latency. Automatically tracks normal variance without manual tuning.
